drills.q: A team enables mypy --strict on their entire existing codebase in one commit and gets hundreds of errors. What went wrong and what's the fix?
drills.a: Strict mode was enabled globally at once on a codebase without existing comprehensive type coverage -- the bundled checks (no untyped defs, no implicit Any) cascade into an avalanche of errors. Fix: scope --strict to already-well-typed modules first via per-module overrides in pyproject.toml, expanding incrementally.

drills.q: A pre-commit config includes the full test suite and commits now take 30+ seconds, so developers use --no-verify routinely. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: A slow, comprehensive check was placed in the fast local per-commit feedback loop where only cheap checks belong -- once commits are slow enough, developers bypass ALL hooks, not just the slow one. Fix: move the full test suite to CI, keep pre-commit scoped to fast checks (ruff lint/format, maybe a narrowly-scoped type check on changed files).

drills.q: Two developers' machines produce different resolved dependency versions from 'the same' requirements.txt. Why, and what's the fix?
drills.a: No lockfile -- pip re-resolves transitive dependencies at install time, which can differ across time/machine even for an identical top-level list. Fix: migrate to a lockfile-based tool (uv) and commit uv.lock so every install resolves to identical pinned versions.

drills.q: A build fails with 'no build backend' errors despite uv managing dependencies fine. What's the cause?
drills.a: [build-system] is missing or misconfigured in pyproject.toml -- uv manages dependencies but delegates actual package building to whatever backend is configured there (hatchling, setuptools, flit-core). These are separate, independently-configured concerns.

drills.q: After migrating from requirements.txt to uv, the resolver produces different transitive dependency versions than the old hand-curated file. Is this a bug, and how should the team handle it?
drills.a: Not necessarily a bug -- a fresh resolver run can legitimately differ from a previously hand-adjusted or older-resolved file, especially with loose constraints. Review the new uv.lock deliberately, run the full test suite against it, and only then commit it as the new source of truth -- or, for a lower-risk migration, pin uv's initial resolution to match the old file's exact versions first, decoupling the tooling change from any dependency-version change.

drills.q: A team's mypy --strict pre-commit hook scans the entire repo on every commit and has become slow. What do you try, in order?
drills.a: First, scope the hook to only changed files (least disruptive). Second, verify mypy's incremental cache is actually being used/persisted between runs. Third, and only as a last resort, move the full-repo strict pass to CI entirely, keeping pre-commit to a fast scoped check or none -- this loses valuable fast local feedback, so it should not be the first response.

drills.q: A team wants to add a large, less-strictly-typed vendored third-party codebase to a project that enforces mypy --strict everywhere. What's the right approach?
drills.a: Add an explicit per-module override excluding or relaxing strictness for that specific vendored path, rather than failing CI on code the team doesn't control or weakening the whole project's strictness bar to accommodate it -- this is exactly the scoping problem per-module overrides exist to solve.

drills.q: pyright and ty both check a codebase and disagree on whether a piece of code is correctly typed. How do you resolve which is 'right'?
drills.a: Check both interpretations against the actual PEP-defined typing specification (PEP 484 and extensions) for the construct in question, since checker behavior is supposed to conform to that shared spec, not either tool's independent judgment. In genuinely ambiguous or under-specified areas, pick one checker as the team's source of truth and stay consistent, rather than trying to satisfy every checker simultaneously.
